newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Zinc set for further run if stocks fall - trade.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Zinc set for further run if stocks fall - trade.

text.p: Zinc prices could be poised for another run-up if London Metal Exchange data due later on Friday show a decline in warehouse inventories, metals traders said.
Stock falls of up to 8,000 tonnes are expected by traders.

The traders said the market was reacting to growing sentiment that world supplies will tighten in the second half of 1997 as the effects of a number of mine closures filter through to consumers. "I wouldn't want to be short zinc," the manager of concentrate sales for an Australian mining house said.
Negotiated terms for treatment and refining fees miners will pay smelters in 1997 should provide a window into the world supply and demand situation, traders said.
A price more favourable to the miners would indicate supplies are tight, with smelters willing to accept less to win business from the mines.
Last year, the mines agreed to pay about US$190 a tonne in fees, a figure the miners maintain would be unrealistically high for 1997 given conditions.
The terms are typically settled in February at an annual meeting of mines and smelters, which this year is being held in Scottsdale, Arizona.
Because of recent curtailments in mine production, mainly among North American mining companies, the miners believe they hold the upper hand in this year's negotiations.
"There just isn't much (concentrates) around," said a buyer for an Asian smelting company.
The shutdown of Anvil Range Mining Corp's Faro Mine in the Yukon for three months from December 20 is seen as a key factor working in favour of the miners.
Stockpiles of ore at the mine are being treated faster than previously anticipated, industry sources say.
There is some talk the mine may not be re-opened on schedule due to metallurgiccal difficulties and equipment problems.

Zinc came under pressure on Thursday to settle US$2.00 a tonne lower as profit-takers zoomed in on what was being perceived as an overbought market, but not before hefty buying swept the three-month contract to a fresh 23-month high of US$1,133 a tonne.
